Model year: 2025-2026 (listed as "Lib Tech 2025-2026") [2] 5. Manufacturer: Mervin Manufacturing [3] 6. Mervin Manufacturing founded: 1977, by Mike Olson and Pete Saari [4] 7. Manufacturing location: Sequim (Carlsborg), Washington, USA [5] 8. Handbuilt in USA: Yes — "Every Lib Tech board is handmade by snowboarders with jobs in the USA" [6] 9. Mervin factory environmental claim: Zero hazardous waste producing factory [7] 10. Mervin ownership: Sold to Altamont Capital Partners in 2013, after being owned by Quiksilver since 1997 [8] 11. Mervin is "the longest running and last major board building factory in the USA" [9] 12. Mervin eco power: 89% of power is generated through wind or water [10] 13. Pro model rider / designer: Travis Rice [2] 14. Board art by: Toby Grubb [11] (NOTE: 2025 model art was by Jessica Lichtenstein — this is the 2026 graphic) 15. Orca originally released: 2018/2019 season (new for 2019) [12] 16. Original release had only one size available: 153cm [13] 17. Model history: The Orca continues from the Climax and Gold Member lineage [14] 18. MSRP (USD): $699.99 [2] 19. Current sale price on lib-tech.com: $489.99 (30% off) [15] 20. Price vs. average snowboard: Costs $131.98 more than the average snowboard price of $468.01 [26] 36. DISAGREEMENT — Flex rating on manufacturer site: 7/10 [2]; Merchant-provided flex: 6/10 [MERCHANT]; SnowboardingProfiles rated flex as "Medium-Stiff (7/10)" on spec but "Flex Feel on Snow: Medium (6/10)" [27]. Comment: The official Lib Tech spec table lists flex as 7. The merchant lists 6/10. SnowboardingProfiles distinguishes between rated flex (7/10) and on-snow feel (6/10). evo calls it "Medium." The Good Ride reviewer calls the flex "stiff" [28]. Multiple sources thus disagree slightly on flex characterization. 37. Available sizes: 138cm, 144cm, 147cm, 150cm, 153cm, 156cm, 159cm, 162cm [2] 38. Sidecut radius (138cm): 6.8m; all other sizes: 7.0m [2] 39. Waist width 150cm: 25.5cm (255mm) [2] 40. Waist width 153cm: 26.7cm (267mm) [2] 41. Nose/tail width 150cm: 30.4 / 29.4 cm [2] 42. Nose/tail width 153cm: 31.6 / 30.5 cm [2] 43. Contact length 150cm: 108cm [2] 44. Contact length 153cm: 110cm [2] 45. Stance range (138cm): 17.5"–22.5" / 2" setback [2] 46. Stance range (147–162cm): 19.5"–24.25" / 2.5" setback [2] 47. Recommended weight 150cm: 120+ lbs / 60+ kg [2] 48. Recommended weight 153cm: 130+ lbs / 65+ kg [2] 49. Taper: 10mm (measured) [29] 50. Setback: 2" (50mm) on 153cm [29] 51. Shape: Tapered Directional [MERCHANT] 52. Board category: All Mountain – Directional [2] 53. Camber type: Orca C2X Directional — rocker between the feet with lengthened camber in nose and tail [30] 54. C2X description: "Shortened rocker section between your feet, with lengthened camber towards the tip and tail" [31] 55. Volume shift: Yes — ride 3–6 cm shorter than normal board [2] 56. Inserts: 2x4 pattern [MERCHANT] 57. Width category: Standard [MERCHANT] 58. Core: HP (Horsepower Construction) — 60% Aspen and 40% Paulownia [32] 59. Laminate: Tri-Ax / Bi-Ax Fiberglass with Basalt Alloy [32] 60. Basalt fiber benefit: "strength properties much higher than fiberglass and better damping properties" [33] 61. Bi-axial fiberglass: 2-way fiber orientation for maximum snap while decreasing chatter [33] 62. Tri-axial fiberglass: "3-way fiber orientation is engineered to increase snap and decrease vibrations" [33] 63. Base: Sintered Knife Cut Base (die-cut to reduce waste) [MERCHANT] 64. Base material: Double layer of ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene [34] 65. Topsheet: Eco Sublimated Poly Topsheet (eco-friendly sublimation process) [MERCHANT] 66. Sidewall: Birch Internal Sidewalls — "Rugged, lightweight, vertical end grain Birch internal sidewalls add pop and durability" [35] 67. Outer sidewall: UHMW Sintered Sidewall — "twice as sintered as most industry sidewalls" [35] 68. Edge technology: Magne-Traction — 7 strategically placed serrations along each edge [25] 69. Tip/tail protection: UHMW Tip/Tail Impact Deflection [MERCHANT] 70. Nose design: Long floaty nose for powder float [2] 71. Tail technology: Whale Tail Technology — "powerful poppy contact maximizing short radius" tail [2] 72. Warranty: 1 year against manufacturer's defects from date of purchase from authorized dealer [36] 73. Warranty coverage: Structural defects only; does NOT cover impact damage, abuse, misuse, or normal wear and tear [37] 74. Warranty restricted: Only applicable to original purchaser; void if purchased from unauthorized dealer (eBay, Craigslist, etc.) [36] 75. Edge hold: "Exceptional" — Magne-Traction provides pronounced grip but doesn't grab like older versions [28] 76. Flex feel on snow: "Stiff" overall — "The middle is nice and stiff. The tail is even stiffer. The nose is not soft either." [28] 77. Pop: "A lot of pop on the ollies and a lot of spring out of the tail" [28] 78. Dampening: "In hard uneven snow, this board absorbs the chatter very well and stays damp" [28] 79. Chunder performance: "A certified chunder buster" in soft uneven snow [28] 80. Switch riding: "Rides better switch than older orcas" with "a more switch friendly tail" [28] 81. Turning: "Very fast edge to edge" with "a turny personality that allows both tight radius turns and long drawn out carves" [28] 82. Speed: "Speed demons and have no issue going fast" [28] 83. Base glide: "Good base glide but it is very wax hungry" [28] 84. Stability at speed: "Exceptional stability in most snow conditions" — "no cause for concern" no matter how fast pushed [38] 85. Buttering: "Still easy to butter because of that rocker" despite stiffness [28] 86. Pipe suitability: "This would be an exceptional pipe board" [28] 87. Powder float: "Exceptional float. It naturally rides nose up and planes through powder easily" [39] 88. Lib Tech website rating: 97% (148 reviews) [2] 89. SnowboardingProfiles.com score: 88.9/100 — Style: Mellow Freeride [27] 90. BoardOfTheWorld editor rating: 4.7 out of 5 [26] 91. BoardOfTheWorld ranking: 2nd out of 38 boards reviewed in all-mountain category [26] 92. Boarderspeak review: 4.0/5.0 — by Tim Schneider, Feb 1 2026 [40] 93. OutdoorGearLab: "Our absolute favorite when it comes to riding steep terrain and deep snow" [38] 94. TheGoodRide (Davey): "This is absolutely a favorite and I am not letting it go" [28] 95. Tactics verified buyer reviews: Overwhelmingly positive — "This is the true one board for all conditions" [41] 96. Merchant-provided customer rating: 5.0 out of 5 (1 review), 100% recommendation rate [MERCHANT] 97. Powder performance: "Perfect for powder" and can work as a dedicated powder board [26] 98. Carving: "Carves beautifully — It has tons of power and response" with "quick turn initiation" [26] 99. Versatility: "Go anywhere, do anything deck" — works in powder, slush, groomers, and ice [26] 100. Stability: "In-control feeling to ride regardless of conditions" [26] 101. Magne-Traction on ice: "Excellent for East Coast ice" per multiple East Coast riders [26] 102. Pressability: "Very pressable / It's perfect for buttering and soft enough to jib in the park" [26] 103. Toe drag elimination: "Wide enough for you to dig your toes in but narrow enough to avoid drag" [2] 104. Tree riding: "Stable and fast to move in the trees" [42] 105. Volume shift advantage: Riders sized down can carve like a bigger board with more maneuverability [42] 106. Base quality criticism: Some users report Lib Tech bases are "some worst in the business" and "not true sintered" — requiring frequent waxing [43] 107. Base wax hunger: Multiple reviewers confirm "very wax hungry" base requiring frequent maintenance [28] 108. Overhyped perception: Forum consensus from some riders: "Great board but over hyped" and "not a do it all everyday board" [44] 109. Magne-Traction grabbiness: Some riders report edges "gets grabby and slow during a carve on soft snow" [45] 110. Switch riding limitation: Directional shape "makes switch riding awkward" for the standard Orca [40] 111. Not ideal for high-speed hardpack carving: "Short effective edge limits grip at speed" [40] 112. Not a true one-board-quiver for most: "For most this won't be a one-quiver-board" [27] 113. Price premium: "There are so many boards that do what the Orca does for much cheaper" [44] 114. Nose interference when playing: Some riders felt "the nose kept getting in the way" during spins [43] 115. Value concern: "Not the best value, as it is one of the more expensive boards" [38] 116. Not for beginners: Board designed for intermediate to expert riders [24] 117. Travis Rice's specs: 5'11", 190 lbs, Size 11 Boots [24] 118. Travis Rice's go-to size: 153 — "Main size for resort, tech trees, Natural Selection" [24] 119. Travis Rice 150: "Fun, tight carving resort board—small but wide enough" [24] 120. Travis Rice 156: "Deep days at resort or backcountry" [24] 121. Travis Rice 159: "Deep pow, mellow terrain" [24] 122. Travis Rice 162: "Extreme deep snow, lower angle terrain" [24] 123. Boot size break down (from TheGoodRide): 147: 7-9, 150: 8-11, 153: 9-12, 156: 10-12, 159: 11-12 [46] 124. Orca (standard) MSRP: $699.99 [2] 125. Golden Orca MSRP: $849.99 [15] 126. Apex Orca MSRP: $1,299.99 [15] 127. Orca Techno Split MSRP: $1,249.99 [15] 128. Golden Orca differs: More switch-friendly power kink tail, volume shift ride 1-3cm shorter (vs 3-6cm for Orca) [47] 129. Apex Orca differs: Techno Pop carbon construction, unidirectional carbon, magnesium fiber, recycled PET core [48] 130. Orca II (upcoming 26/27): Rounded nose for easier turning, improved switch-ability in tail, recycled ocean-bound top sheet, Makah Hemlock core [49] 131. Key competitors: Ride Warpig, Never Summer Harpoon, Salomon Dancehaul, Jones Flagship, Jones Mind Expander, Jones Hovercraft, Capita Mercury, Gnu Gremlin, Korua Dart, Yes Hybrid, Bataleon Party Wave II [50] 132. Ride Warpig comparison: Warpig has more freestyle approach; Orca drifts closer to freeriding [51] 133. Ride Warpig price: MSRP ~$529.95, notably cheaper than the Orca [52] 134. Jones Flagship comparison: "Orca is a more playful powder board"; "Flagship dominates more in technical and advanced backcountry lines" [53] 135. Never Summer Harpoon: Described as "Orca clone" — "not-so-subtly-named" competitor [51] 136. Capita Mercury and Salomon Assassin: Better for all-mountain carving with camber-dominant profiles [40] 137. Gnu Gremlin: Within Mervin family; has C3 camber between feet vs Orca's C2X rocker — better edge hold for aggressive riding on hardpack [54] 138. Golden Orca vs Orca: "If you don't ride switch a lot, get an Orca. If you ride switch a lot, get a Golden Orca" [55] 139. SwitchbackTravel places Orca in All-Mountain/Powder category alongside Ride Warpig and Never Summer Swift [56] 140. Charitable contribution: Portion of each Orca sale donated to Orca Conservancy for Salish Sea Southern Resident Killer Whales [2] 141. Eco topsheet: Water-based eco-sublimation process (no toxic solvents) [57] 142. Eco base: Sintered knife-cut base die-cut to reduce waste [MERCHANT] 143. Core wood: Aspen and Paulownia — lightweight and sustainable species [32] 144. Factory environmental practices: Zero hazardous waste, low VOC epoxy, eco materials [7] 145. Eco materials used: "non-petroleum based bio-plastics, soy-based elastomer sidewalls, low VOC epoxy, additive-free basalt fibers, and FSC 'pure' certified wood cores" [10] 146. Gender: Unisex / Men's (no specific women's version of the Orca) [22] 147. Rider level: Intermediate to Advanced/Expert [24] 148. Terrain focus: Freeride, Powder, All Mountain [MERCHANT] 149. Best use case: Powder and tree board to add to quiver; can handle resort conditions well [27] 150. Ideal conditions: Deep powder, variable snow, trees, steep terrain [38] 151. Specialist vs generalist: "A specialist that happens to generalize reasonably well, not a true all-mountain board" [40] 152. Recommendation if powder < 50% of days: "There may be better options for your quiver" [40] 153. East Coast viability: "Absolutely still worth it if you don't get to ride powder that often" due to Magne-Traction ice performance [26]
